senses.definition: The direct and immediate results of a change on the thing you changed.
senses.caution: Naming something as first order is a promise that you have thought about what comes after it, and the next question in a senior room is always what comes after it. It also collides with first-order approximation, which means roughly, so in a mixed room say which you mean before someone hears you say the number is a guess.
senses.example: The first order effect is that reviews get faster. What I actually care about is what happens to review quality once they do.

cues.text: A sponsor asks what the automation will do, and you want a term for the immediate, intended result before anyone asks what comes next.
In a design review you want to separate the direct consequence of a change from everything it sets off downstream.
You are writing a business case and want to label the obvious, countable benefit separately from the speculative ones.
You are talking about a tax on sugary drinks and want the name for what it does straight away to prices, as distinct from what happens after.

distractors: A loop in which each turn makes the next one easier and the whole thing speeds up.
The small set of things you know to be true once precedent has been stripped away.
A kind of input or output a system works in, such as text, images, audio or video.
Weight and seriousness in how a person carries themselves.
A slice of the market defined by the industry it serves.

senses.definition: The later results that follow once people and systems adapt to the first change.
senses.caution: It is the easiest phrase in the language to use as a veto. Raise it and you should be able to name one, or you have added doubt to someone else's proposal without paying anything for it. People notice when it only ever arrives on other people's ideas.
senses.example: The second order effect is the one I'd watch: once reviewers trust the tool, they stop reading the diffs.

cues.text: A proposal will obviously save time, and your worry is what people will quietly stop doing carefully once it does.
You are asking a team to think past the immediate benefit of a new incentive to how people will behave once they work out how it is measured.
In a risk review you want the phrase for harm that only appears after everyone has adapted to the new system.
A road near you is being widened, and you want the phrase for how traffic tends to grow to fill it.
A friend describes a rule their building introduced, and you want the term for what residents promptly started doing to get around it.

distractors: The place where raw tables and columns are mapped onto the words the business uses.
A funded, staffed team that concentrates a scarce skill in one place and sets how it works.
Temporary structure that holds work up until the real thing can stand without it.
To work over the exact phrasing of something already drafted.
The most senior people in a firm, spoken of as one group.
